note:
James identifies himself as a slave of God and of Christ. A bondservant (text note) is one purchased and owned by a master or “lord.” This indicates not only humility on the part of the writer but a profound testimony to his conversion to faith in his earthly half-brother as his Redeemer (1 Cor. 15:3). James is a servant to both God and Jesus, a crucial theological bracketing.

**to the twelve tribes in the Dispersion.** A reference not only to Jewish Christians scattered outside of Israel but also to Gentile Christians, who have become ingrafted into Christ, the true Israel, so that they also have become, along with Jewish Christians, the continuation of true Israel (cf. Gal. 3:16, 29; 6:15, 16; Rev. 7:1–9). This theme also appears in 1 Peter, where Peter similarly addressees “the elect exiles of the Dispersion” (1:1). The addressees of 1 Peter are certainly not only Jewish Christians but also Gentile believers (as is apparent from 1 Pet. 2:10 [cf. Rom. 9:24–26] and 2:18, where “servants” are likely Gentiles). Thus, to speak of “the elect exiles of the Dispersion” of 1 Pet. 1:1 is likely a way of referring to the Jewish-Gentile church as the continuation of true Israel, since Israel was formerly called exiles because they were dispersed from Babylon in the OT epoch. The same thing is the case in James 1:1.

A call to understand suffering from the vantage point of confidence in God’s sovereignty. What follows requires careful thinking from a theological perspective.

**brothers.** Fellow believers are addressed in familial terms, as is fitting for those who have God as their Father.

**trials.** Various kinds of trying circumstances, often related to persecution such as the early Christians endured.

Trials can be considered pure joy only when there is knowledge that they are designed by God for a purpose. They are tests of faith given in order to develop perseverance. In turn, perseverance produces mature Christian character (Rom. 5:3).

To be wise in biblical terms is to know and understand godliness, to do what is pleasing to God (Heb. 5:14). Chapter 3 elaborates this theme.

**ask God.** God is the source of wisdom. He grants it to those who sincerely seek it from Him.

This rare expression was possibly coined by James. It suggests a man who has two souls; he is as unstable as a person with a split personality, since he claims to have faith but, in reality, he is a doubter (v. 6).

Both the poor and the rich are exhorted to take pride in their positions. The poor brother is wealthy in spiritual treasure. He has high status in the kingdom of God. If the term “rich” refers to wealthy Christians, James means they can rejoice that they have learned where true treasure is found. If “rich” refers to the ungodly, the reference to their “boast” is ironic., 10

Echoes the prophetic oracles of salvation used by OT prophets and by Jesus (Matt. 5:3–11). The “crown of life” that is “promised” by God could be translated as “crown that is life,” likely referring to the future reward of resurrection. The “crown of life” (i.e., reward of resurrection) is also promised to those who persevere through trial in Rev. 2:10. This crown is not something that is earned; rather, it is the gift to those who turn from their own righteousness and rest only in Christ (Rom. 6:23). Such faith necessarily perseveres (John 6:35–40; Rom. 8:28–30; Phil. 1:6), resulting in the full experience of new life in the final resurrection from the dead.

There is an important difference between the concepts “test” and “tempt.” God tests people, but never tempts them in the sense of enticing them to sin. Jesus, in the wilderness, was tested by God and tempted by Satan. There is also a difference between temptations that arise from our own sinful inclinations (internal) and those coming from without (external). Jesus, being free of original sin, was tempted externally but not internally. The testing of our faith may be the occasion for temptations to come, both internal and external, yet the temptations never have God as their author.

Nature’s luminaries vary in magnitude and are subject to phases, eclipses, and shadows. God is the ultimate Author of light. In Him, there are no changes of brightness or clarity. There is no fluctuation in His character.

Lit. “gave birth to us.” This refers to the grace of regeneration by which we are adopted into God’s family (1 Pet. 1:23). This “giving of birth” is regeneration, which is end-time new creation. That new creation is in mind is further evident from observing that the regenerate believers are “a kind of firstfruits of his creatures,” that is, the beginning renewal of the whole creation that will eventually be completely restored. This new life that believers experience in the here and now is the beginning stage of new resurrection life that will be consummated at the very end of the age in physical resurrection (v. 12 note). The idea is much like that of Rom. 8:18–23, where Christians who have begun to experience resurrection life through the Spirit (Rom. 8:11–15) are called “the firstfruits of the Spirit,” and await their physical resurrection, at which time the whole creation will be renewed.

**by the word of truth.** Regeneration is the monergistic work of the Spirit of God—He alone grants new birth to His people (cf. John 3:1–15 and notes). However, He does this work by taking the Word of God, both read and preached, and applying it effectually to the hearts of His elect. This verse is a clear indication of the primacy of grace in James’s theology. Only by the Spirit’s work through the gospel are we brought to new life.

verse_quote: quick to hear, slow to speak.
note: Though the Christian community places high regard on the talent of eloquent speech, James places the accent on listening. It is the person who listens intently to the Word of truth who progresses in godliness.
True hearing of the Word must lead to godly action.
In the ancient world, mirrors were made of polished metal, not glass. Scripture is a mirror of the soul’s need for grace. It reveals our true character to us.

James uses this phrase as a synonym for sacred Scripture (Ps. 19:7).

**liberty.** The law of God sets us free, as it drives us to Christ who alone can free us from sin. Having been justified, we then find God’s law to be the law of freedom, for we are truly free only when we do what is pleasing to the Lord (John 8:36; Rom. 8:2, 15; Gal. 3:15–29; 5:13).
See ch. 3.

verse_quote: Religion that is pure and undefiled.
note: James emphasizes concern for widows and orphans as a true measure of obedience that is pleasing to God. It reflects the concerns of God Himself (Deut. 10:18; Ps. 9:18 note; 68:5; 146:9). Israel was given this responsibility in the OT (Deut. 14:29; Ezek. 22:7).

The expression is similar to that found in Gal. 2:6. James forbids having a respect for persons based purely on externals. A respect grounded only in externals is contrary to the behavior of God, who is no respecter of persons (Rom. 2:11; Eph. 6:9; Col. 3:25). In the light of Christ’s divine glory, it is foolish to show favoritism based on inferior levels of human glory.

**Lord Jesus Christ, the Lord of glory.** This may be rendered “our Lord Jesus Christ, the glory.” Here Jesus may be identified with the glory of God. He is Immanuel, “God with us,” the dwelling of God with man.

Though God calls us to discern and to discriminate between good and evil, discrimination based on mere externals such as economic status, racial or ethnic differences, and the like is considered an evil form of judgment.

Inheritance in the kingdom is based on God’s sovereign election. He chooses not according to merit or worldly status. The standards of this world have no influence on God’s gracious election (1 Cor. 1:28, 29; Eph. 1:4). The text does not warrant any form of “poverty mysticism” by which poverty in itself renders a person good in God’s sight (Ps. 9:18 note).

The verb is a strong word and is used to refer to the oppressive work of Satan (Acts 10:38). The rich used political and judicial power to exploit the poor and needy of the nation. As a group, the rich have a strong tendency to rely upon wealth and power rather than to find their redemption in Christ.

The supreme law of God.

**love your neighbor.** James regards the sin of favoritism as a violation of the great commandment (Lev. 19:18; Deut. 6:5; Matt. 22:36–39), making the perpetrator a lawbreaker. James, like Paul (Rom. 13:8–10), says that love of neighbor is the fulfillment of the law (that is, of the last six of the Ten Commandments).

This text does not negate the biblical concept of gradation of evil. Some sins are more heinous than others and receive a more severe punishment than sins that are “less” heinous (Matt. 11:21, 22; Luke 12:47, 48; John 19:11; Heb. 10:29). However, even in the smallest sin, a serious offense is made against God. To sin at one point is to sin against the law and therefore against the Lawgiver. Even the smallest sin is worthy of hellfire, and every impenitent person goes to hell, though some in hell receive a greater punishment than others. James, like Jesus, warns against a superficial understanding of the law of God (Matt. 5:17–20).

Cf. Zech. 7:9; Matt. 5:7; 18:21–35. Though God is never obligated to show mercy, He freely chooses to do so in abundance. He reserves the divine prerogative to show mercy upon whom He wills (Rom. 9). By His law, however, we are commanded to temper justice with mercy. He warns that if we refuse to show mercy, we will not receive mercy from Him.

This introduces the crucial issue of the relationship between faith and works. The question under scrutiny is, “What kind of faith is saving faith?” James’s question is rhetorical; the obvious answer is that faith without works cannot save. Faith that yields no deeds is not saving faith. The NT does not teach justification by works, but it also does not teach justification by the profession of faith or the claim to faith; it teaches justification by the possession of true faith, and true faith always bears the fruit of love of God and neighbor. James has in mind a genuine, living faith that produces fruitful works, which is evidence that will vindicate (or prove) the validity of one’s authentic justifying faith at the last judgment. See Introduction: Special Issues.
Describes a “faith” of words without actions., 16

When Luther and the Reformers insisted on the formula _justification by faith alone_, they meant to insist that justification rests upon reliance on the merit of Christ alone. The “alone” does not mean that the faith exists alone without any subsequent fruit of obedience. Luther insisted that saving faith is a living faith. We are justified by faith alone but not by a faith that is alone, namely, a faith that consists only of a profession without the fruit of loving service to God and neighbor. “Dead” faith does not mean a faith that has perished; rather, the image suggests a faith that never had any true life in it to begin with. A dead faith cannot make one alive, cannot “save your souls” (1:21), and is therefore false and useless.

James challenges anyone who claims to have faith to demonstrate it, to make it visible. Deeds of obedience make up the only evidence of saving faith that is visible to human eyes. God can see the heart, but our only view of the heart is by the sight of outward fruit.

verse_quote: You believe that God is one.
note: To believe that God is one can be a mere intellectual assertion. To believe _in_ God requires personal trust. To believe that He is one only entails assenting to a proposition even the demons acknowledge, and the “faith of demons” saves no one. Saving faith includes cognitive knowledge but goes beyond it to personal trust and submission.

This is a strong rebuke. It is a moral judgment more than an intellectual judgment, recalling the judgment that falls upon “the fool” in the Wisdom Literature of the OT.

**useless.** Barren of fruit.

James appeals to Abraham as his chief exhibit of one whose faith is justified, or demonstrated, by his works. This involves no conflict with Paul, who also appeals to Abraham as the chief exhibit of one justified, or declared righteous in the Lord’s sight, by faith alone. Note that James appeals to Gen. 22, while Paul appeals to Gen. 15. In the sight of God, Abraham is justified in Gen. 15, long before he offers Isaac on the altar. God knew Abraham’s faith to be genuine. Abraham is justified to us, to human eyes, in Gen. 22 when he shows his faith through his obedience. Jesus used the same verb in Luke 7:35 when He declared “wisdom is justified by all her children” (i.e., shown to be genuine wisdom by its results). Here, the word “justify” does not mean to be reconciled to God and declared righteous in His sight, but it means to demonstrate the truth of a prior claim. Just as true wisdom is demonstrated by its fruit, Abraham’s claim to faith is justified by fruit, namely, his outward obedience. His works were not the meritorious cause of his salvation; they added no merit to the perfect and sufficient merit of Christ. The same is true of our good works.
The full outworking of faith is seen in works. True faith always produces fruit. Faith and works may be distinguished, but never separated or divorced.

A person is not shown to be just by the mere profession of faith or by having a faith that remains alone, never producing any good works. The validity of one’s profession is evident to other people only by what one does. None of our deeds are worthy of ultimate justification in the sight of God. Only the merit of Christ avails for that kind of justification, for that declaration of righteousness in His sight. Only by trusting in Christ alone can we be declared righteous in the sight of God. Here James attacks all forms of antinomianism that seek to have Jesus as Savior without embracing Him as Lord. Just as Paul demonstrated that trusting in one’s own works is deadly, so James teaches that resting on empty or dead faith is deadly. See theological note “Faith and Works” above.

James echoes Jesus’ emphasis on the crucial importance of the use of words in daily life (Matt. 12:36; Mark 7:20–23).

**3:1 judged with greater strictness.** James gives a sober warning concerning the responsibility of teachers. Teachers exert influence over trusting students, a relationship that makes the students vulnerable to serious error. The teacher is held in strict account for what he or she teaches. This strict judgment should restrain teachers from careless words. The tongue of the teacher can be a devastating peril. The early church gave high esteem to the office of the teacher (Matt. 5:19; 18:6; cf. Rom. 14:10–12).

James uses metaphors from common experience to illustrate his cardinal point that great results can be achieved by small means. The tongue is a small part of the body that is capable of creating great disasters.

An uncontrolled tongue is likened to a fire that rages out of control (Ps. 120:3, 4; Prov. 16:27).

**staining.** Evil speech (including blasphemy, gossip, slander, lying, false vows, and the like) has the power to spoil, stain, and corrupt the entire moral character of a person.

verse_quote: no human being can tame the tongue.
note: The tongue is harder to tame than wild beasts. It is filled with poison more venomous than a viper’s (Ps. 58:4; 140:3; Rom. 3:13, 14).

The tongue is capable of use for both virtue and vice. The same mouth uses the tongue for these contradictory purposes.

**made in the likeness of God.** See theological note “Human Beings Created in the Image of God” on p. 13. Our speech is one of the ways that we are made in God’s image, and we should use our words in ways that reflect God’s own Word, which in turn honors and “blesses” Him and others.
Note the similarity here between James’s metaphors and those used by Jesus in Matt. 7:16., 12

Just as James exhorts believers to demonstrate their faith through works, so he also calls for the demonstration of wisdom by godly living. The one who is truly wise in the Lord will “show his works” or “fruit” (cf. v. 17) by blessing with the mouth and not cursing (cf. again 3:10–12).

**meekness.** The sign of wisdom is a gentle and humble spirit. As arrogance and foolishness go together, so do humility and wisdom.
Envy and covetousness poison the spirit. They are linked to self-centered and self-serving ambition. These vices blind one to true understanding and wisdom, and are contrary to the love of neighbor.
Divine wisdom is set in bold contrast to the wisdom of this world. The wisdom of the flesh reflects the deception of Satan and is foolishness in the sight of God.

As James earlier showed that the tongue is capable of creating disastrous evil, so here he emphasizes the destructive power of envy and selfish ambition. From them flow all kinds of evil, including vandalism, murder, adultery, warfare, theft, slander, and other sins that violate people and provoke chaos in the community.

Wisdom that is a gift of God (1:5) reflects the purity of God Himself. Again, wisdom is linked to godliness as God Himself is the source and fountainhead of true wisdom.

**peaceable.** This is authentic peace, free of a quarrelsome attitude.

**gentle.** Thoughtful and respectful of other people’s feelings.

**open to reason.** Willing to listen to and obey others.

**full of mercy.** The wise person is not stingy in mercy but demonstrates charity in broad measure.

**good fruits.** Those who partake of God’s true “wisdom from above” will bear “good fruits” because they have been “brought forth (regenerated) as “firstfruits” of the beginning new creation (1:18). Those who are part of the new creation will bear new, “good fruits.”

**impartial and sincere.** The wise person is fair and without deception, deceit, or fraud.

The fruit reaped by the planting of wisdom is a bountiful crop of righteousness. These “righteous” fruits of true believers, which are “sown” by God (cf. 1:18), will be “harvested” at the very end of the age and will indicate that such people had authentic faith throughout the course of their believing life (cf. 2:14–26). One of these fruits is that of “peace,” one of the telltale signs of the inbreaking new creation that will be consummated at the final harvest (cf. e.g., Gal. 6:15, 16).
James probes the root cause of divisions among the saints. They are caused by evil desires. Envy is still in view as an evil desire that is destructive.

That is, “you do not ask” from “God, who gives generously to all” (1:5). Envy is a sin against God. It flows from a lack of gratitude toward God who bestows gifts upon His people. It also results from a failure to seek one’s own gifts from God rather than from the world.
God refuses to grant our petitions when they proceed from evil desires. To pray from wrong motives is not to pray in faith (Rom. 14:23; Heb. 11:6).

Spiritual infidelity is in view here. The OT often saw that Israel’s idol worship was adultery, since it was showing covenantal loyalty to something of this creation instead of to the Creator, who was the husband of Israel (e.g., Jer. 3:9; Ezek. 16; 23:37; Hos. 4:13; cf. Rev. 2:20–22). This is illicit spiritual intercourse and thus adultery. To be “a friend of the world” is to be more committed to the “world” than to God and thus to align oneself with the evil world system against God and His people. There is no spiritual neutrality.

James probably does not have one specific text in mind, so he is making a general reference to a common biblical theme, as is also seen in Matt. 2:23. The idea may derive partly from Ex. 20:5 and Deut. 4:24. If the verse is understood as speaking of the human spirit, James is thinking of texts such as Gen. 6:3 and 8:21, which are about the consequences of original sin.
Cf. Prov. 3:34.

This requires a willing act of accepting the authority of God, for we are under His authority whether we bow willingly to Him or not. Here “submit” means “to obey.”

**Resist the devil, and he will flee.** Satan is not equal in power or authority to God. Though Satan is powerful, he is not invincible. He flees from saints who wear the armor of God and who resist him (see Eph. 6:10–17).

verse_quote: Be wretched and mourn and weep.
note: A call to genuine repentance by which we mourn for our sins.

A sin of speech, slander flows out of envy and reflects the work of Satan. The Gk. word for “devil” means “slanderer.” Slandering other Christians destroys fellowship and breaks the royal law. When we speak falsely against a fellow believer, we speak not only against the person but against the law of God. The slanderer sets himself illicitly as a judge above the law (v. 12).
James rebukes the person who lives life and makes future plans without any regard for the providence of God. Such a person lives without regard for divine sovereignty., 14
The word “if” refers to future events that are conditional. Here the primary consideration in all future planning is the will of the sovereign God.

Boasting of one’s own power and accomplishments is evil. The Christian is to boast only in the Lord (2 Cor. 11:30; 12:5, 9). For “what do you have that you did not receive? If then you received it, why do you boast as if you did not receive it?” (1 Cor. 4:7). It is arrogance not to live our lives in awareness that in God “we live and move and have our being” (Acts 17:28). Such arrogance superficially exalts the human to a position that only God can hold.
The sins of neglect and of omission are in view here.

The Bible nowhere condemns wealth itself. In fact, it is often viewed as the blessing of God (Prov. 10:22). However, the rich, as a social class, may sometimes be guilty of exploiting and oppressing the poor. Many of them may live as if there is no God who rules over everything (4:13–17 note). God reserves severe judgment for those who live in such a manner (Luke 6:24).

Earthly treasures are subject to decay and eventually perish. James here echoes the teaching of Jesus (Matt. 6:20).

**last days.** The latter days predicted in the OT have begun with the coming of Christ (cf. Acts 2:17; 1 Cor. 10:11; Gal. 4:4; Heb. 1:1–4; 9:26; 1 John 2:18) and will continue until they are consummated at Christ’s final coming (cf. Heb. 9:28; 1 Pet. 1:5). Here, the careless rich do not realize that they are living in these last days, which may be consummated at any moment, at which time the final judgment will occur. “To lay up treasure” for oneself, which will corrode away, “will be evidence against” them on the last day that will lead to their judgment., 3
This is a violation of the law of God. Wages are not only to be paid, they are to be paid on time (Lev. 19:13; Deut. 24:14, 15).

Like animals fattened for slaughter, the rich are unaware of the disaster awaiting them at the final judgment. “The day of slaughter” is another reference to their final judgment. Just as cows are oblivious to their own coming slaughter and fatten themselves up, so it is with their unbelieving human counterparts, who suffer an even worse judgment. On the contrary, Christians are exiles in this present age (James 1:1; 1 Pet. 1:1; 5:13) and should always be living patiently with an eye on their coming permanent home in the eternal new heavens and earth (cf. v. 7 note; Heb. 11:13–16), where nothing will fade away or corrode.

The unjust use of power often causes the death of innocent people. The verse could also be understood figuratively, since to rob people of their wages and livelihood is to commit a kind of murder against them.
The saints require patience as they await God’s promised vindication of His people. God promises justice to correct prevailing forms of injustice in this world (Luke 18:1–8).

verse_quote: Judge is standing at the door.
note: This verse reflects the urgent sense of the nearness of Christ’s coming. The “coming of the Lord” could happen at any time. James is echoing the NT’s hope of the return of Jesus at the end of the age. James may also be thinking of the radical nearness of judgment facing every person, for in light of eternity, the life of every person, no matter his age, will soon be over and then every person will stand before the judgment of God (cf. v. 3, where James mentions the “last days.”). Professing believers may themselves be revealed as pseudo-believers and be judged if they have not “strengthened” their hearts (cf. v. 8) and demonstrated genuine faith by bearing fruit (2:14–26; 3:17, 18). Indeed, this is a warning of judgment to the church community (cf. Matt. 7:15–23) and not at this point to unbelieving pagans. Perseverance and patience is demanded in the face of the promised “coming of the Lord” that “is at hand.” That is, Christ’s final coming could occur at any time.
The prophets and especiallyJob are examples to be followed by the hearers who have just been exhorted to have patience in vv. 7–9., 11

This emphatic exhortation signals a weighty priority for godliness. To exalt refraining from false oaths and vows to a high level of priority may seem strange to some, but it is consistent with the biblical concern for covenant-keeping and the sanctity of the faith.

**do not swear.** This is not a prohibition against cursing or the use of vulgarity. It concerns taking oaths by appealing to objects as witnesses (which in biblical terms is a form of idolatry). Only God can be an omnipresent, omniscient witness to oaths and vows, so to call upon mere objects as witnesses is to reject the Creator in favor of that which is created. Just and godly vows are not prohibited in Scripture because they form a vital part of all covenants. The only vows that are prohibited are vows to commit a sin, vows sworn the name of anyone else besides the Lord, and vows that one does not intend to keep (cf. Num. 30; Deut. 23:21–23).

**“yes” be yes.** The Christian is expected to be a person whose word can be trusted. James’s teaching here echoes that of Jesus in the Sermon on the Mount (Matt. 5:34–37).

**that you may not fall under condemnation.** Here again is another exhortation to the believing community to persevere in godly behavior, so that they will not “fall under condemnation” of final judgment. Once more, people are to make sure of the genuineness of their faith by bearing fruit. This time the fruit of speaking righteously is highlighted, as in 3:1–12. If they do not persevere, they may find themselves to be of another character than that which they profess, and accordingly judged as an unbeliever.
See topical article “Worship” on p. 2383.

See Acts 14:23; Titus 1:5.

**anointing him with oil.** Olive oil was commonly used in medicine in the ancient world (Mark 6:13; Luke 10:34). The oil may also have a symbolic reference to the healing power of God.

There is no special “prayer of faith” that has inherent healing power. Instead, the power of trusting and faithful prayer is accented here; the Christian community should be devoutly engaged in intercessory prayer for the sick. This verse is the classic proof text for the institution of the Roman Catholic sacrament of the anointing of the sick (formerly “extreme unction”). The anointing of the sick is a healing rite that, (administered along with the sacraments of the Eucharist and penance), has come to be thought of primarily as the “last rites” in preparation for death. However, while this text may include the notion that death may occur and that the prayer of faith is appropriate at death, James’s point is that the church should pray for the healing and the life of the ill person, so that “the Lord will raise him up.” Thus, the passage is not about a sacramental anointing. Furthermore, as James has already said, sometimes faith’s calling is to be joyful and steadfast under “trials of various kinds” (1:2–4), trials that may include serious and prolonged illness. Even as the Christian offers this prayer in faith, he must remember that God is sovereign over life and death, including his own (cf. 4:13–17). Care must be taken, then, not to isolate this statement from the teaching of the rest of the letter.

**committed sins.** Sin and illness are not unrelated, though illness is not always the consequence of specific sins. Forgiveness is therapeutic to the body as well as to the soul.

Though confession to a priest is not required by Scripture, confession to God and to one another is. Overreaction against the Roman Catholic sacrament of penance may lead to a neglect of authentic godly confession to one another, confession that can bring healing and renewed vitality to the soul.

**righteous person.** A godly person who prays in faith is a just or righteous person.

Though Elijah held the special office of OT prophet, he shares a common humanity with all believers. His effectual prayer life is therefore a model for all the saints of God, that is, all of those who trust in Jesus alone for salvation., 18
To stray into sinful patterns of thought and behavior.

The care of the souls of the community is a matter of concern for every member, not only church officers or the clergy. Mutual help and encouragement are required.

**cover.** Refers to God’s covering of sins with forgiveness (Ps. 32:1; 85:2), for in the repentance and faith by which a wayward sinner is returned to the Lord, God pardons the sinner’s transgressions.
